items.meaning: A gentle way to suggest an activity or plan to someone.
items.example: How about we grab a coffee next week to discuss the project?
items.plain: Let's grab a coffee next week to discuss the project.
items.note: Very common, friendly way to propose an idea. Can be used in many contexts.

items.meaning: Asking if someone is available to do something specific.
items.example: Are you free to meet up for lunch sometime next month?
items.plain: Can you meet up for lunch sometime next month?
items.note: A polite and direct way to check availability for a specific activity.

items.meaning: Asking if a proposed time, date, or plan is convenient for the other person.
items.example: I was thinking of Tuesday evening; does that work for you?
items.plain: I was thinking of Tuesday evening; is that convenient for you?
items.note: Standard phrase for confirming arrangements. Very versatile and polite.

items.meaning: Asking someone what they are currently doing or what their plans are.
items.example: Hey, what are you up to this weekend? Fancy catching a movie?
items.plain: Hey, what are your plans this weekend? Fancy catching a movie?
items.note: Informal and friendly. Can refer to current activity or future plans.

items.meaning: An informal and friendly way to suggest meeting up.
items.example: It's been a while; fancy getting together for a drink soon?
items.plain: It's been a while; would you like to meet for a drink soon?
items.note: Common in British English, but understood in American English. Casual and warm.

items.meaning: Introducing a suggestion or a plan you've been considering.
items.example: I was thinking of hosting a small dinner party next Saturday.
items.plain: I'm considering hosting a small dinner party next Saturday.
items.note: A gentle way to float an idea, inviting feedback or agreement.

items.meaning: Asking someone to inform you about something, often their decision or availability.
items.example: I'm free on Friday; let me know if that day works for you.
items.plain: I'm free on Friday; tell me if that day works for you.
items.note: Very common and useful for making flexible plans. Polite and open-ended.

items.meaning: Expressing a strong suggestion or intention to do something together.
items.example: We should definitely try that new restaurant everyone's talking about.
items.plain: We must try that new restaurant everyone's talking about.
items.note: Enthusiastic and encouraging. Often used when making future plans.

items.meaning: Indicating that you are willing to consider other people's ideas or proposals.
items.example: I'm not sure what to do for my birthday; I'm open to suggestions.
items.plain: I'm not sure what to do for my birthday; I welcome your ideas.
items.note: Friendly and collaborative, inviting others to contribute.

items.meaning: Asking someone about their free time or when they can meet.
items.example: Before I suggest a date, what's your availability like next week?
items.plain: Before I suggest a date, when are you free next week?
items.note: A polite and slightly more formal way to inquire about someone's schedule.

items.meaning: Asking if someone is able to attend an event or meet at a specific time.
items.example: The party starts at seven; could you make it then?
items.plain: The party starts at seven; can you be there then?
items.note: Common for checking attendance or punctuality. Polite and direct.

items.meaning: Stating the specific days or times when you are available.
items.example: I'm free on Wednesday evening if you want to grab dinner.
items.plain: Wednesday evening works for me if you want to grab dinner.
items.note: Simple and direct way to communicate your availability.

items.meaning: Suggesting a tentative plan or appointment that can be confirmed later.
items.example: We don't have to commit now, but let's pencil something in for next month.
items.plain: We don't have to commit now, but let's make a tentative plan for next month.
items.note: Implies flexibility and that the plan isn't set in stone yet.

items.meaning: Promising to look at your schedule to confirm availability for a proposed plan.
items.example: That sounds good; I'll check my calendar and get back to you.
items.plain: That sounds good; I'll look at my schedule and get back to you.
items.note: Standard response when you need to verify your schedule before committing.

items.meaning: Asking for feedback or agreement on a suggestion or plan you've just made.
items.example: We could meet at the cafe around three; how does that sound?
items.plain: We could meet at the cafe around three; is that acceptable?
items.note: A very common and polite way to invite a response to a proposal.

items.meaning: A polite and common way to invite someone to do something.
items.example: Would you like to come over for dinner on Saturday?
items.plain: Do you want to come over for dinner on Saturday?
items.note: Versatile for invitations, offers, and suggestions. Polite and standard.

items.meaning: Expressing a strong desire for someone to participate in an activity or event.
items.example: I'd love for you to join us for the picnic in the park.
items.plain: I really want you to join us for the picnic in the park.
items.note: A warm and enthusiastic way to extend an invitation.

items.meaning: Announcing an event or gathering that you are hosting.
items.example: We're having a small get-together at our place next Friday.
items.plain: We are hosting a small get-together at our place next Friday.
items.note: Direct and common way to inform someone about an event.

items.meaning: Extending an open invitation, indicating that someone is free to participate.
items.example: If you're free, you're welcome to join us for brunch on Sunday.
items.plain: If you're free, you can join us for brunch on Sunday.
items.note: Friendly and inclusive, often used for informal gatherings.

items.meaning: An informal invitation for someone to visit your home for a specific purpose.
items.example: Why don't you come over for a board game night next week?
items.plain: Why don't you visit my home for a board game night next week?
items.note: Casual and friendly, typically used among friends.

items.meaning: A very polite and indirect way to make a request or extend an invitation.
items.example: I was wondering if you'd be free to grab a coffee sometime soon.
items.plain: Would you be free to grab a coffee sometime soon?
items.note: Softens the request, making it less demanding. Good for sensitive topics.

items.meaning: A formal and very polite way to express pleasure at someone's potential attendance.
items.example: We'd be delighted if you could attend our anniversary celebration.
items.plain: We would be very happy if you could attend our anniversary celebration.
items.note: Quite formal, suitable for significant events or when addressing esteemed guests.

items.meaning: A direct way to ask about someone's availability to attend an event.
items.example: We're having a barbecue on Saturday; are you free to come?
items.plain: We're having a barbecue on Saturday; can you come?
items.note: Straightforward and common for informal invitations.

items.meaning: A direct invitation to participate in an activity or event with a group.
items.example: We're heading to the park; join us for a walk if you like.
items.plain: We're heading to the park; come with us for a walk if you like.
items.note: Simple, friendly, and inclusive. Can be used spontaneously.

items.meaning: Announcing that you are organizing and holding an event at your home or venue.
items.example: I'm hosting a small gathering next weekend, just a few friends.
items.plain: I am organizing a small gathering next weekend, just a few friends.
items.note: Clear and direct way to inform someone about an event you are putting on.

items.meaning: An enthusiastic and polite way to accept an invitation or suggestion.
items.example: "Would you like to come to the concert?" "Yes, I'd love to!"
items.plain: "Would you like to come to the concert?" "Yes, I would really like to!"
items.note: Very common, warm, and positive acceptance.

items.meaning: Expressing positive agreement or enthusiasm for a suggestion or plan.
items.example: "How about dinner on Friday?" "That sounds great!"
items.plain: "How about dinner on Friday?" "That is a good idea!"
items.note: A very common and versatile positive response.

items.meaning: A formal and very polite way to accept an invitation.
items.example: "We'd love you to join us." "Thank you, I'd be delighted to."
items.plain: "We'd love you to join us." "Thank you, I would be very happy to."
items.note: More formal than "I'd love to," suitable for more formal invitations.

items.meaning: An informal and enthusiastic way to confirm your participation in an activity.
items.example: "We're going hiking on Saturday." "Sounds fun, count me in!"
items.plain: "We're going hiking on Saturday." "Sounds fun, I'll join!"
items.note: Casual and friendly, often used among friends.

items.meaning: A polite and standard way to acknowledge and express gratitude for being invited.
items.example: Thanks for the invitation to your party; I'm really looking forward to it.
items.plain: I appreciate you inviting me to your party; I'm really looking forward to it.
items.note: Essential for polite social interaction, whether accepting or declining.

items.text: I'm really looking forward to it
items.form: I'm really looking forward to it
items.meaning: Expressing eager anticipation for a future event or meeting.
items.example: Thanks for inviting me to the concert; I'm really looking forward to it.
items.plain: Thanks for inviting me to the concert; I'm very excited about it.
items.note: A common and warm way to show enthusiasm for an upcoming event.

items.meaning: Confirming that a proposed time, date, or plan is entirely suitable and convenient.
items.example: "How about meeting at 7 PM?" "Yes, that works perfectly for me."
items.plain: "How about meeting at 7 PM?" "Yes, that time is completely suitable for me."
items.note: A strong and clear affirmation of suitability.

items.meaning: Giving a strong assurance that you will attend an event or meeting.
items.example: Don't worry, I'll definitely be there for your presentation.
items.plain: Don't worry, I will certainly attend your presentation.
items.note: Conveys commitment and reliability.

items.meaning: A warm and enthusiastic way to accept a suggestion or invitation.
items.example: "Would you like to join us for a walk?" "Oh, I'd love that!"
items.plain: "Would you like to join us for a walk?" "Oh, I would really enjoy that!"
items.note: Similar to "I'd love to," but often used as a standalone response.

items.meaning: An informal way to express agreement with a proposed plan or suggestion.
items.example: "So, we'll meet at the cafe at two?" "Yep, sounds like a plan!"
items.plain: "So, we'll meet at the cafe at two?" "Yep, that's a good plan!"
items.note: Casual and friendly, often used to finalize informal arrangements.

items.meaning: A polite and common way to decline an invitation or request.
items.example: I'm afraid I can't make it to the party on Saturday.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I cannot come to the party on Saturday.
items.note: A standard softener for delivering bad news or a refusal.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly more formal way to decline an invitation or request.
items.example: Unfortunately, I'm not able to attend the meeting next week.
items.plain: Sadly, I cannot attend the meeting next week.
items.note: Suitable for both formal and informal contexts, conveying regret.

items.meaning: A common and straightforward reason for declining an invitation.
items.example: Thanks for the invite, but I already have plans that evening.
items.plain: Thanks for the invite, but I am busy that evening.
items.note: A simple and generally accepted reason for unavailability.

items.meaning: Suggesting the possibility of meeting or doing the activity at a later date.
items.example: I can't make it this weekend, but maybe another time soon?
items.plain: I can't make it this weekend, but perhaps we can meet another time soon?
items.note: Softens a refusal and keeps the door open for future plans.

items.meaning: Expressing sincere regret before delivering a refusal or bad news.
items.example: I'm really sorry but I won't be able to join you for dinner.
items.plain: I apologize, but I won't be able to join you for dinner.
items.note: A strong apology, indicating genuine regret for the refusal.

items.text: I won't be able to make it
items.form: I won't be able to make it
items.meaning: A common and polite way to state that you cannot attend an event.
items.example: Thanks for the invitation, but I won't be able to make it to the party.
items.plain: Thanks for the invitation, but I cannot come to the party.
items.note: Standard and clear way to decline attendance.

items.meaning: Expressing strong gratitude, often used before declining an invitation.
items.example: Thanks so much for thinking of me, but I'm already booked.
items.plain: I really appreciate you thinking of me, but I'm already booked.
items.note: Softens the refusal by emphasizing appreciation for the invitation.

items.meaning: Explaining that you are busy or committed to another activity.
items.example: I'm tied up with work commitments all next week, unfortunately.
items.plain: I am busy with work commitments all next week, unfortunately.
items.note: A common and natural way to explain unavailability due to other obligations.

items.meaning: Complimenting the invitation or idea before explaining why you cannot accept.
items.example: It sounds wonderful but I'm afraid I have a prior engagement.
items.plain: That sounds wonderful but I'm afraid I have a prior engagement.
items.note: A polite softener, showing appreciation for the offer even if you can't accept.

items.text: I'll have to take a rain check
items.form: I'll have to take a rain check
items.meaning: Politely declining an invitation but suggesting to do it another time.
items.example: I can't make it tonight, but I'll have to take a rain check.
items.plain: I can't make it tonight, but let's do it another time.
items.note: Very common idiom for postponing. Implies genuine interest in meeting later.

items.meaning: A formal apology followed by a reason for being unable to attend.
items.example: My apologies, I'm already booked for that evening.
items.plain: I apologize, I already have an appointment for that evening.
items.note: Polite and clear, suitable for slightly more formal contexts.

items.meaning: Expressing regret that you are unable to accept an invitation or do something.
items.example: I wish I could join you for the concert, but I have to work late.
items.plain: I regret that I cannot join you for the concert, as I have to work late.
items.note: Conveys genuine desire to participate despite inability.

items.meaning: Expressing appreciation for someone's thoughtfulness or generosity.
items.example: That's very kind of you to invite me, but I'm not feeling well.
items.plain: It's thoughtful of you to invite me, but I'm not feeling well.
items.note: A polite way to acknowledge an invitation, often used before declining.

items.text: I'm not sure I can commit
items.form: I'm not sure I can commit
items.meaning: Expressing uncertainty about being able to promise attendance or participation.
items.example: I'm not sure I can commit to the weekly book club right now.
items.plain: I'm uncertain if I can promise to attend the weekly book club right now.
items.note: A gentle way to express hesitation without a firm refusal.

items.meaning: A warm welcome to guests, encouraging them to feel comfortable and relaxed.
items.example: Come in, come in! Make yourself at home, the drinks are in the fridge.
items.plain: Come in, come in! Feel comfortable and relaxed, the drinks are in the fridge.
items.note: Standard welcoming phrase for guests in your home.

items.meaning: Offering refreshments or assistance to a guest.
items.example: Please sit down. Can I get you anything to drink?
items.plain: Please sit down. Would you like something to drink?
items.note: A polite and hospitable offer to guests.

items.meaning: A polite expression of gratitude from a guest to a host.
items.example: As I was leaving, I said, "Thanks for having me, it was a lovely evening."
items.plain: As I was leaving, I said, "Thank you for inviting me, it was a lovely evening."
items.note: Essential phrase for guests when leaving someone's home.

items.text: It was lovely to see you
items.form: it was lovely to see you
items.meaning: A warm farewell expression, indicating pleasure at having met or spent time together.
items.example: "Goodbye!" "You too, it was lovely to see you again."
items.plain: "Goodbye!" "You too, I enjoyed seeing you again."
items.note: Common and friendly closing remark for social interactions.

items.meaning: Expressing sincere gratitude for someone's actions or presence.
items.example: I really appreciate you coming all this way for my birthday.
items.plain: I am very grateful that you came all this way for my birthday.
items.note: A warm and heartfelt way to show thanks.

items.text: Let me know if you need
items.form: let me know if you need
items.meaning: Offering help or assistance, inviting the other person to ask if necessary.
items.example: If you're staying overnight, let me know if you need an extra blanket.
items.plain: If you're staying overnight, tell me if you need an extra blanket.
items.note: A polite and helpful offer, showing consideration for a guest.

items.meaning: Reassuring someone, especially a guest, that they don't need to be concerned or help.
items.example: "Can I help with the dishes?" "No, don't worry about a thing, I'll do them later."
items.plain: "Can I help with the dishes?" "No, don't be concerned, I'll do them later."
items.note: A kind and hospitable phrase to put guests at ease.

items.meaning: Offering assistance with tidying or cleaning after a meal or gathering.
items.example: That was a delicious meal; I'll help clear up the table.
items.plain: That was a delicious meal; I will help tidy the table.
items.note: A polite and helpful offer from a guest to a host.

items.meaning: A polite response to "Thank you" or a general expression of enjoyment.
items.example: "Thanks for coming!" "It was a pleasure, I had a wonderful time."
items.plain: "Thanks for coming!" "I enjoyed it, I had a wonderful time."
items.note: Versatile, can be used by host or guest. Slightly more formal than "no problem."

items.meaning: A common greeting used to ask about someone's well-being since the last meeting.
items.example: Long time no see! How have you been since we last met?
items.plain: Long time no see! How are you since we last met?
items.note: Standard and friendly way to catch up with someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.text: What have you been up to
items.form: What have you been up to
items.meaning: Asking someone about their recent activities, experiences, or news.
items.example: It's great to see you! What have you been up to lately?
items.plain: It's great to see you! What have you been doing lately?
items.note: A very common and natural way to initiate a catch-up conversation.

items.meaning: An informal way to express that a very long time has passed since the last meeting.
items.example: Wow, it's been ages since we last saw each other!
items.plain: Wow, a very long time has passed since we last saw each other!
items.note: Casual and friendly, used among people who know each other well.

items.meaning: Suggesting a more in-depth meeting to discuss recent events and news.
items.example: This is too quick; we should catch up properly over coffee soon.
items.plain: This is too quick; we should meet for a longer chat over coffee soon.
items.note: Implies that a brief encounter isn't enough to share everything.

items.meaning: Inviting someone to share the full details of a story or experience.
items.example: I heard you got a new job; tell me all about it!
items.plain: I heard you got a new job; please share all the details!
items.note: Enthusiastic and encouraging, shows genuine interest.

items.text: I was just thinking of you
items.form: I was just thinking of you
items.meaning: Expressing that someone was recently on your mind, often when you unexpectedly meet them.
items.example: What a coincidence! I was just thinking of you the other day.
items.plain: What a coincidence! I was thinking about you the other day.
items.note: A warm and friendly phrase, often used when bumping into someone.

items.meaning: A general inquiry about someone's life, work, and overall well-being.
items.example: It's good to see you! How's everything going with the new project?
items.plain: It's good to see you! How are things with the new project?
items.note: A versatile and common way to start a conversation or catch up.

items.meaning: Expressing pleasure at meeting or seeing someone again.
items.example: Hi Sarah, it's good to see you after all this time!
items.plain: Hi Sarah, I'm happy to see you after all this time!
items.note: A standard and warm greeting, suitable for various social contexts.

items.meaning: Asking someone to keep you updated with information or developments.
items.example: Let me know how the plans for the trip progress; keep me in the loop.
items.plain: Let me know how the plans for the trip progress; keep me updated.
items.note: Informal and common, implies you want to stay informed.

items.text: We must do this again soon
items.form: we must do this again soon
items.meaning: Expressing a strong desire to repeat the social activity or meeting in the near future.
items.example: That was a lovely evening; we must do this again soon.
items.plain: That was a lovely evening; we should meet again soon.
items.note: A warm and friendly closing remark, indicating enjoyment and future intent.

items.meaning: Introducing a frank or sincere opinion, sometimes a slightly critical one.
items.example: To be honest, I wasn't entirely happy with the service at that restaurant.
items.plain: Frankly, I wasn't entirely happy with the service at that restaurant.
items.note: A common discourse marker, often used to soften a potentially negative comment.

items.meaning: A slightly softer way to introduce a frank or personal opinion.
items.example: If I'm being honest, I found the movie a bit disappointing.
items.plain: Frankly, I found the movie a bit disappointing.
items.note: Similar to "to be honest," but the "if" adds a touch more politeness.

items.meaning: Introducing a request for more specific information or to confirm understanding.
items.example: Just to clarify, are we meeting at seven or seven-thirty?
items.plain: To confirm, are we meeting at seven or seven-thirty?
items.note: Useful for ensuring mutual understanding and avoiding miscommunication.

items.meaning: Introducing a contrasting or alternative point of view or consideration.
items.example: The restaurant is a bit pricey, but on the other hand, the food is excellent.
items.plain: The restaurant is a bit pricey, but the food is excellent.
items.note: A common discourse marker for presenting a balanced perspective.

items.meaning: Introducing a contrasting point or qualification after a previous statement.
items.example: It was a tough week. Having said that, I did manage to finish the report.
items.plain: It was a tough week. However, I did manage to finish the report.
items.note: Used to add a nuance or counterpoint to what was just stated.

items.meaning: Clarifying or softening a previous statement, often by rephrasing or adding context.
items.example: I mean, it's not that I don't want to go, I just have too much work.
items.plain: I don't want to go, but I just have too much work.
items.note: A common filler and softener, used to explain or qualify.

items.meaning: Introducing a tentative or slightly hesitant suggestion or interpretation.
items.example: I suppose you could say the party was a success, despite the rain.
items.plain: The party was a success, despite the rain.
items.note: A softener, indicating a degree of uncertainty or modesty in the statement.

items.meaning: Expressing uncertainty or difficulty in giving a definitive answer or opinion.
items.example: "Will they come?" "It's hard to say, they're usually quite busy."
items.plain: "Will they come?" "I'm not sure, they're usually quite busy."
items.note: A common way to acknowledge uncertainty without committing to an answer.

items.meaning: Gently disagreeing with an extreme statement or strong opinion.
items.example: "That was the worst movie ever!" "I wouldn't go that far, but it wasn't great."
items.plain: "That was the worst movie ever!" "I don't agree completely, but it wasn't great."
items.note: A polite way to express partial disagreement or temper an exaggeration.

items.meaning: Clarifying or rephrasing a previous statement to ensure better understanding.
items.example: I'm not saying it's bad; what I mean is, it could be improved.
items.plain: I'm not saying it's bad; I mean, it could be improved.
items.note: Useful for explaining oneself more clearly, especially if misunderstood.

items.meaning: Asking if someone wants to do something or join an activity.
items.example: Would you be interested in joining us for dinner next Saturday?
items.plain: Do you want to join us for dinner next Saturday?
items.note: A polite and open-ended way to invite someone, suggesting an option rather than a demand.

items.meaning: Suggesting a specific time or date for a plan, often when other options are difficult.
items.example: I'm quite busy, but let's try for next Tuesday evening if that works for you.
items.plain: I'm quite busy, but can we aim for next Tuesday evening?
items.note: Used when proposing a specific time, implying flexibility might be limited.

items.meaning: Indicating that one's schedule is adaptable and open to various times or dates.
items.example: I'm pretty flexible next week, so just let me know what day suits you best.
items.plain: My schedule is open next week, so tell me what day is best.
items.note: A common, friendly way to show willingness to accommodate others' schedules.

items.meaning: Asking someone to specify their preferred time for a meeting or activity.
items.example: I'm free all afternoon, so what time suits you for our coffee?
items.plain: I'm free all afternoon, so tell me what time is best for our coffee.
items.note: A direct but polite way to ask about someone's availability.

items.meaning: Promising to provide updates or further information as it becomes available.
items.example: The plans aren't firm yet, but I'll keep you posted on any changes.
items.plain: The plans aren't firm yet, but I will tell you about any changes.
items.note: Common in informal and semi-formal contexts when details are still developing.

items.meaning: Expressing strong enthusiasm or eagerness to do something.
items.example: I'm really keen to try that new restaurant, so thanks for the invitation!
items.plain: I'm very eager to try that new restaurant, so thanks for the invitation!
items.note: Shows genuine enthusiasm; common in both British and American English.

items.meaning: Expressing willingness or pleasure to do something.
items.example: I'd be happy to bring a dessert if that would be helpful for the party.
items.plain: I would gladly bring a dessert if that would help for the party.
items.note: A polite and helpful way to offer assistance or accept a request.

items.meaning: Suggesting an alternative or backup plan, often when the primary option is difficult.
items.example: If the weather is bad, we could always have the picnic indoors at my place.
items.plain: If the weather is bad, we can have the picnic indoors at my place.
items.note: Used to propose a less ideal but still viable option.

items.meaning: Giving permission or encouraging someone to bring something, like a guest or an item.
items.example: Feel free to bring a friend along to the barbecue if you like.
items.plain: You can bring a friend along to the barbecue if you like.
items.note: A welcoming phrase used by a host to make guests feel comfortable.

items.meaning: Expressing a desire or hope for something to happen, often an activity with others.
items.example: It would be great to catch up properly soon, perhaps over coffee next week.
items.plain: I would really like to catch up properly soon, perhaps over coffee next week.
items.note: A warm and friendly way to suggest future plans or express a wish.

items.meaning: Politically expressing regret when stating an unavoidable obligation or refusal.
items.example: I'm afraid I have to decline your invitation as I'll be out of town.
items.plain: I regret that I must decline your invitation as I'll be out of town.
items.note: A polite and common way to deliver bad news or a refusal.

items.meaning: Politically stating that one already has a commitment or appointment.
items.example: I'm so sorry, but I have a prior engagement that evening and can't make it.
items.plain: I'm so sorry, but I already have something planned that evening.
items.note: A formal and polite way to decline an invitation without giving too many details.

items.meaning: Explaining that one has two appointments or commitments scheduled for the same time.
items.example: Unfortunately, I'm double booked for that time, so I'll have to miss the meeting.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I have two things scheduled for that time, so I'll miss the meeting.
items.note: A common, slightly informal way to explain a scheduling conflict.

items.meaning: Politically declining an invitation or opportunity.
items.example: That sounds like fun, but I'll have to pass on the hiking trip this weekend.
items.plain: That sounds like fun, but I cannot go on the hiking trip this weekend.
items.note: A casual but clear way to decline, often used among friends.

items.text: I'm not feeling up to it
items.form: I'm not feeling up to it
items.meaning: Explaining that one lacks the energy or desire to do something, often due to tiredness or illness.
items.example: I'm not feeling up to it tonight, so I think I'll stay home instead of going out.
items.plain: I don't have the energy tonight, so I think I'll stay home instead of going out.
items.note: A common, gentle way to decline due to personal well-being.

items.meaning: Expressing regret or disappointment about being unable to do something.
items.example: It's a shame I can't join you for the concert, as I already bought tickets for another show.
items.plain: I'm disappointed I can't join you for the concert, as I already bought tickets for another show.
items.note: Conveys regret without over-apologizing, often used when declining.

items.meaning: Expressing sincere enjoyment and gratitude after an event or visit.
items.example: Thank you for inviting me; I had a wonderful time at your dinner party.
items.plain: Thank you for inviting me; I really enjoyed myself at your dinner party.
items.note: A standard and warm phrase used by a guest to thank a host.

items.meaning: Expressing willingness to provide something or help financially for a shared activity.
items.example: I'm happy to contribute to the cost of the food for the picnic.
items.plain: I am willing to pay for some of the food for the picnic.
items.note: A polite way to offer to share expenses or provide items for a group event.

items.meaning: A friendly and informal way to ask someone how they are doing generally.
items.example: It's been a while! How's life treating you these days?
items.plain: It's been a while! How are you doing these days?
items.note: A warm, slightly more reflective way to ask "How are you?"

items.meaning: Asking someone to provide details or updates about a situation or recent events.
items.example: It's been ages, so please fill me in on everything you've been up to.
items.plain: It's been ages, so please tell me all the details about what you've been doing.
items.note: Informal and friendly, used when catching up with someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.meaning: Expressing satisfaction or relief that something long-awaited or desired is now happening.
items.example: It's great to finally meet you in person after all our emails.
items.plain: I'm very happy to meet you in person after all our emails.
items.note: Used when an anticipated event or meeting is taking place.

items.meaning: Expressing happiness or relief that a shared activity or meeting was possible.
items.example: I'm so glad we could find a time to get together; it's been too long.
items.plain: I'm very happy we found a time to meet; it's been too long.
items.note: A warm and appreciative phrase, often used at the beginning or end of a social gathering.

items.text: It's good to hear from you
items.form: It's good to hear from you
items.meaning: Expressing pleasure at receiving communication from someone, often after a period of silence.
items.example: Oh, hi Sarah! It's good to hear from you; I was just thinking about you.
items.plain: Oh, hi Sarah! I'm happy you contacted me; I was just thinking about you.
items.note: A standard, friendly greeting when someone calls, texts, or emails after a gap.

items.meaning: Introducing a question or topic that one has intended to bring up for some time.
items.example: I've been meaning to ask you about your new job; how's it going?
items.plain: I wanted to ask you about your new job; how's it going?
items.note: A natural way to transition to a new topic or ask a specific question.

items.meaning: Introducing a related topic that comes to mind because of the current conversation.
items.example: We were talking about travel; speaking of which, have you booked your summer holiday yet?
items.plain: We were talking about travel; on that topic, have you booked your summer holiday yet?
items.note: A common discourse marker to smoothly shift to a related subject.

items.meaning: Redirecting the conversation to a previous topic after a digression.
items.example: Anyway, getting back to our plans for the weekend, what did you decide?
items.plain: So, returning to our plans for the weekend, what did you decide?
items.note: Used to steer the conversation back to the main point after a tangent.

items.meaning: Asking to recall the last point of a conversation after an interruption or digression.
items.example: Sorry, my phone rang. Where were we before I was interrupted?
items.plain: Sorry, my phone rang. What were we talking about before I was interrupted?
items.note: A common phrase to resume a conversation smoothly.

items.text: To cut a long story short
items.form: To cut a long story short
items.meaning: Introducing a summary of a lengthy explanation or narrative.
items.example: To cut a long story short, we ended up missing our flight but still made it to the wedding.
items.plain: In summary, we missed our flight but still made it to the wedding.
items.note: Used to get to the main point quickly, implying there's more to the story.

items.meaning: A friendly, informal greeting used when encountering someone after a long period.
items.example: Oh, Mark! Long time no see! How have you been?
items.plain: Oh, Mark! I haven't seen you in a long time! How have you been?
items.note: Very informal and friendly, suitable for close acquaintances.

items.meaning: Asking about the progress or development of a situation or plan.
items.example: How are things shaping up with your move to the new apartment?
items.plain: How is your move to the new apartment progressing?
items.note: A natural way to inquire about ongoing plans or projects.

items.meaning: Asking for the most recent news or developments concerning a particular person or situation.
items.example: What's the latest with your sister's job search? Has she found anything?
items.plain: What is the newest information about your sister's job search?
items.note: A common, informal way to ask for updates.

items.meaning: Expressing a desire to learn or understand something.
items.example: I'm curious to know what you thought of the new art exhibition.
items.plain: I want to know what you thought of the new art exhibition.
items.note: A polite and engaging way to ask a question, showing genuine interest.

items.meaning: Expressing eagerness to receive information or an opinion from someone.
items.example: I'm keen to hear all about your recent trip to Japan when we next meet.
items.plain: I'm eager to hear all about your recent trip to Japan when we next meet.
items.note: Shows strong interest in what someone has to say.

items.meaning: Stating one's readiness to attend a meeting or social gathering.
items.example: I'm available to meet any time after 3 PM on Friday.
items.plain: I can meet any time after 3 PM on Friday.
items.note: A clear and direct way to communicate one's availability.

items.meaning: Suggesting that people compare their calendars to find a mutually convenient time.
items.example: It's hard to find a time for everyone, so let's coordinate our schedules soon.
items.plain: It's hard to find a time for everyone, so let's compare our calendars soon.
items.note: A slightly more formal or business-like way to suggest finding a meeting time.

items.meaning: Expressing willingness to assist with tasks or preparations.
items.example: If you need an extra pair of hands for setting up, I'm happy to help out.
items.plain: If you need an extra pair of hands for setting up, I am willing to assist.
items.note: A friendly and common offer of practical assistance.

items.meaning: Promising to phone someone, often to finalize plans or catch up.
items.example: I'll give you a call tomorrow to sort out the details for the weekend.
items.plain: I will phone you tomorrow to sort out the details for the weekend.
items.note: A common, informal way to arrange future communication.

items.text: I'll confirm closer to the date
items.form: I'll confirm closer to the date
items.meaning: Promising to finalize attendance or details nearer to the event day.
items.example: I'm not sure about my work commitments yet, so I'll confirm closer to the date.
items.plain: I'm not sure about my work commitments yet, so I will finalize my attendance nearer the date.
items.note: A polite way to express uncertainty while keeping an option open.

items.meaning: Promising to communicate with someone again soon.
items.example: It was great catching up; I'll be in touch next week about our plans.
items.plain: It was great catching up; I will contact you next week about our plans.
items.note: A polite and common way to end a conversation, indicating future communication.

items.text: Would you care to join us
items.form: Would you care to join us
items.meaning: A polite way to invite someone to an activity or event.
items.example: We're heading to the new gallery opening; would you care to join us?
items.plain: We're going to the gallery opening; would you like to come?
items.note: Very polite and slightly formal, suitable for new acquaintances or more formal invitations.

items.meaning: Suggesting to arrange details for a future meeting or activity.
items.example: I'd love to catch up next week. Let's make a plan soon.
items.plain: I want to meet next week. Let's arrange the details soon.
items.note: Common, friendly way to initiate or follow up on arranging a social event.

items.text: I'm happy to go with the flow
items.form: I'm happy to go with the flow
items.meaning: Expressing willingness to adapt to whatever plans others decide.
items.example: I don't have a strong preference for dinner, I'm happy to go with the flow.
items.plain: I don't mind what we do for dinner, I'll adapt to your choices.
items.note: Shows flexibility and an easygoing attitude, useful when others are making decisions.

items.meaning: Suggesting a general timeframe for when to meet or complete something.
items.example: We need to discuss the project. Let's aim for next week to meet.
items.plain: We should try to meet next week to discuss the project.
items.note: A common way to propose a general time without committing to a specific day yet.

items.meaning: Offering to organize the details for an event or meeting.
items.example: Don't worry about the restaurant booking, I'll make the arrangements.
items.plain: I will book the restaurant, you don't need to worry about it.
items.note: A helpful offer when hosting or taking initiative in planning a social gathering.

items.meaning: Asking someone to provide updates as new information becomes available.
items.example: Let me know if the plans change for Saturday, keep me posted.
items.plain: Tell me if the plans for Saturday change.
items.note: Informal and direct, used among friends or close colleagues.

items.meaning: Expressing strong interest in receiving additional information or details.
items.example: Your trip sounds fascinating, I'm keen to hear more about it.
items.plain: Your trip sounds interesting, I really want to hear more details.
items.note: Shows genuine interest in a conversation topic, encouraging the other person to continue.

items.meaning: Offering to contribute money or effort to a shared expense or task.
items.example: If you're buying the tickets, I'm happy to chip in for the cost.
items.plain: I'll gladly contribute money for the tickets if you buy them.
items.note: Common and friendly, often used for shared expenses or group efforts.

items.meaning: Offering to contribute food or drink to a social gathering.
items.example: Thanks for inviting me to the potluck, I'll bring something to share.
items.plain: I'll bring some food or drink for everyone at the potluck.
items.note: A polite and common offer when attending a casual meal or party.

items.meaning: Indicating that one has definite, unchangeable commitments.
items.example: I'd love to come, but I have firm plans that evening.
items.plain: I want to come, but I already have definite commitments for that evening.
items.note: A polite but clear way to decline an invitation, suggesting the plans cannot be changed.

items.meaning: Promising to respond or provide information at a later time.
items.example: I need to check my schedule, I'll get back to you by tomorrow.
items.plain: I will check my schedule and reply to you by tomorrow.
items.note: Standard phrase for deferring a response, common in both social and professional contexts.

items.meaning: Suggesting to make contact briefly to discuss something or catch up.
items.example: Things are busy now, but let's touch base soon about that project.
items.plain: We should talk briefly soon about that project.
items.note: Often used in professional settings but also common among friends for quick updates.

items.meaning: Expressing that a significant amount of time has passed since the last meeting.
items.example: Oh, Sarah! It's been too long, how have you been?
items.plain: Sarah! We haven't seen each other in a very long time, how are you?
items.note: A warm, friendly greeting used when reuniting with someone after a long absence.

items.meaning: A general inquiry about someone's life and circumstances.
items.example: It's great to see you! How have things been since we last met?
items.plain: It's good to see you! What has been happening in your life?
items.note: A common, friendly way to start a conversation and catch up with someone.

items.meaning: Asking for updates on recent events or changes in someone's life.
items.example: We haven't spoken in a while, what's new with you?
items.plain: We haven't talked recently, tell me what has happened in your life.
items.note: A casual and direct way to initiate catching up with a friend or acquaintance.

items.text: I'm glad we could make it work
items.form: I'm glad we could make it work
items.meaning: Expressing satisfaction that a plan or meeting was successfully arranged despite difficulties.
items.example: With our busy schedules, I'm glad we could make it work for dinner tonight.
items.plain: Given our busy schedules, I'm happy we managed to arrange dinner tonight.
items.note: Used after successfully coordinating plans, especially when there were challenges.

items.meaning: A polite and warm way to express enjoyment after a conversation or meeting.
items.example: Thanks for the coffee, it was lovely catching up with you.
items.plain: Thank you for coffee, I really enjoyed talking and getting updated with you.
items.note: A common closing remark after a social interaction, especially with friends.

items.meaning: Expressing sincere pleasure and satisfaction with an experience.
items.example: Thank you for the party, I really enjoyed myself.
items.plain: I had a wonderful time at your party.
items.note: A common and heartfelt way to thank a host or express appreciation for an event.

items.meaning: A polite expression of gratitude to a host for inviting one to their home.
items.example: The dinner was delicious, thanks for having me over.
items.plain: The dinner was delicious, thank you for inviting me to your home.
items.note: Standard polite phrase used when leaving someone's home after a visit.

items.meaning: Confirming attendance at a specific location for an event or meeting.
items.example: Great, so the concert starts at eight. I'll see you there!
items.plain: Okay, the concert begins at eight. I will meet you at the venue!
items.note: A common and casual way to confirm plans and express anticipation for meeting.

items.text: I'm looking forward to seeing you
items.form: I'm looking forward to seeing you
items.meaning: Expressing anticipation and pleasure about an upcoming meeting with someone.
items.example: Our dinner plans sound great, I'm looking forward to seeing you on Friday.
items.plain: Our dinner plans are good, I'm excited to meet you on Friday.
items.note: A warm and friendly way to end a conversation about future plans.

items.meaning: Suggesting to choose a specific day and time for a future meeting or event.
items.example: We should definitely get together soon. Let's set a date next week.
items.plain: We should meet soon. Let's choose a specific day and time next week.
items.note: A common phrase for moving from a general intention to concrete planning.

items.text: I'm happy to host this time
items.form: I'm happy to host this time
items.meaning: Offering to be the host for a social gathering on a particular occasion.
items.example: You hosted last time, so I'm happy to host this time.
items.plain: You were the host last time, so I'd like to host now.
items.note: A polite and reciprocal offer, often used among friends who take turns hosting.

items.meaning: Offering to contribute a sweet course to a meal or gathering.
items.example: What can I bring to dinner? I'll bring a dessert.
items.plain: What should I bring to dinner? I will bring a sweet dish.
items.note: A common and polite offer when attending a dinner party or potluck.

items.text: I'm not sure I can make it
items.form: I'm not sure I can make it
items.meaning: Expressing uncertainty about being able to attend an event.
items.example: Thanks for the invitation, but I'm not sure I can make it.
items.plain: Thank you for inviting me, but I don't know if I can attend.
items.note: A soft and polite way to indicate potential unavailability without a firm decline.

items.meaning: Promising to inform someone about something in the future.
items.example: I need to check my calendar, I'll let you know by tomorrow morning.
items.plain: I will check my calendar and inform you by tomorrow morning.
items.note: A standard phrase for deferring a response, common in both social and professional contexts.

items.meaning: Expressing that one has an overwhelming amount of work to do.
items.example: I'd love to join, but I'm swamped with work this week.
items.plain: I want to come, but I have too much work to do this week.
items.note: A common and understandable reason for declining social invitations.

items.meaning: A polite way to explain that one has two conflicting appointments.
items.example: I'm afraid I'm double-booked that evening, so I can't make it.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I have two appointments at the same time that evening, so I can't come.
items.note: A polite and common way to decline an invitation due to a scheduling conflict.

items.meaning: Offering to pay for the next set of drinks or food for the group.
items.example: You got the last one, so I'll get the next round.
items.plain: You paid last time, so I will pay for the drinks this time.
items.note: Common in casual social settings like bars or cafes, showing generosity.

items.meaning: Offering to pay for something, usually a meal or drinks, for others.
items.example: Don't worry about the bill, it's on me tonight.
items.plain: Don't worry about the bill, I will pay for it tonight.
items.note: A casual and generous offer, often used among friends or when treating someone.

items.meaning: Suggesting a casual meeting to talk and update each other while having coffee.
items.example: It's been a while, let's catch up over coffee next week.
items.plain: We haven't met in a while, let's meet for coffee next week to talk.
items.note: A very common and informal way to suggest a casual social meeting.

items.meaning: Making contact to see how someone is doing or to get an update.
items.example: Hi, I'm just checking in to see how you're doing.
items.plain: Hello, I'm contacting you to see how you are.
items.note: A friendly and informal way to initiate contact, often by phone or message.

items.meaning: Indicating general availability during the evening hours on most days.
items.example: I'm pretty flexible next week; I'm free most evenings.
items.plain: I'm quite flexible next week; I am available on most evenings.
items.note: Useful for giving a general idea of availability without listing specific days.

items.text: What are your thoughts on that
items.form: What are your thoughts on that
items.meaning: Asking for someone's opinion or perspective on a particular topic.
items.example: We're thinking of going to the new Italian place, what are your thoughts on that?
items.plain: We're considering the new Italian restaurant, what do you think about it?
items.note: A polite way to invite input and ensure everyone's opinion is considered.

items.meaning: Expressing willingness to change the time or date of a planned event.
items.example: If that time doesn't work for you, I'm happy to reschedule.
items.plain: If that time is not convenient for you, I am willing to change our meeting time.
items.note: Shows flexibility and consideration for the other person's availability.

items.meaning: Promising to send a short message or email to someone.
items.example: I'll drop you a line later with the details for the party.
items.plain: I will send you a short message later with the party details.
items.note: An informal and friendly way to say you'll contact someone, usually in writing.

items.text: I'm looking forward to hearing from you
items.form: I'm looking forward to hearing from you
items.meaning: Expressing anticipation for a response or communication from someone.
items.example: Let me know your availability soon, I'm looking forward to hearing from you.
items.plain: Please tell me your availability soon, I am eager to receive your reply.
items.note: A polite closing remark in an email or conversation when awaiting a response.

items.text: I'm happy to pick you up
items.form: I'm happy to pick you up
items.meaning: Offering to collect someone by car from their location.
items.example: If you don't want to take a taxi, I'm happy to pick you up.
items.plain: If you prefer not to take a taxi, I can collect you by car.
items.note: A kind and practical offer, especially when someone might have difficulty with transport.

items.text: I'm just about to head out
items.form: I'm just about to head out
items.meaning: Indicating that one is preparing to leave their current location very soon.
items.example: I can't talk long, I'm just about to head out for dinner.
items.plain: I cannot talk for long, I am leaving for dinner very soon.
items.note: Used to politely shorten a conversation when one needs to depart.

items.meaning: Informing someone that one will arrive slightly after the scheduled time.
items.example: Sorry, I'm running a little late, I'll be there in ten minutes.
items.plain: Apologies, I will be slightly delayed, I'll arrive in ten minutes.
items.note: A common and polite way to communicate a minor delay when meeting someone.
